notes.1: Candidates tackled this question reasonably well. They found part (a) the most challenging. Parts (b) and (c) were very well done.
notes.1a: This question was well answered. Candidates need to make better use of the Periodic Table provided. Some candidates did not realise that Xenon was a noble gas in part (i) and some struggled with the compound that is used to neutralise acidic soil. Most recognised that carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas but many could not recognise the ionic compounds.
notes.1b: This part was answered really well. The most common mistake was using the formula of hydrogen instead of water.
notes.1c: This part was answered really well. Candidates should be encouraged to re-read the sentence or paragraph again after fitting in the words to check that the sentence makes sense.
notes.2: Parts of this question were attempted to a high standard; however the responses to part (b) were less well answered.
notes.2a: Most candidates gave the correct answer for this part. Some candidates did not use the diagrams and preferred to say the ‘energy was taken in’. Candidates were explicitly asked to use the experiment shown and not just the definition.
notes.2b: This part showed that many candidates did not know how to make pure dry crystals. Few candidates started by adding one substance to another from a burette and using an indicator. Most chose to start from ‘heating the substances together’. This led to many candidates describing evaporating all the water away, which would leaving a powder rather than crystals.
notes.2c: Most candidates knew something about fermentation. There were a few candidates who did not appreciate that yeast will be denatured at higher temperatures.
notes.2d: There were some candidates who drew ‘methanol’ and ‘propanol’ instead of ‘ethanol’ and some missed out hydrogens and bonds completely.
notes.2e: Most candidates identified at least one of the two answers for this part.
notes.3: This question was answered reasonably well in parts (a) and (b). In part (c)(i) many candidates missed that it was a ‘salt’ that was formed. In part (d) candidates often did not identify the correct state of matter.
notes.3a: (i) This part was answered very well.
notes.3aii: This was well answered for most candidates. The common error was to suggest ‘neutralisation’.
notes.3b: This part was very well done. The candidates knew the pH scale.
notes.3c: (i) Few candidates did well with this part. Most mentionedr ‘water’ but few identified the second word ‘salt’ and chose a chemical substance instead.
notes.3cii: Not many correct answers were seen here. Some candidates misinterpreted the question and many talked about ‘yeast’ instead of baking powder.
notes.3iii: The majority of candidates did not realise that if the sodium hydrogen carbonate was impure it could cause us harm.
notes.3d: Some candidates knew that carbon dioxide is a gas under normal conditions and gave this as their answer. Many candidates did not read the question properly and so did not use the ‘kinetic particle theory’ as required.
notes.4: This question was answered successfully in most cases. Part (a) was very well answered and showed that candidates knew their apparatus. Most candidates could interpret the graph in part (b)(i). Many candidates did not read the graph in part (ii) or were not precise enough. Many candidates could draw the correct line on the graph for a higher temperature in part (b)(iv). The electrolysis in part (d) was answered well and showed the candidates were comfortable with this part of the syllabus.
notes.4a: The vast majority of candidates answered this part correctly.
notes.4b: (i) Some candidates did not realise that they needed to talk about the ‘volume of gas remaining constant’ as well.
notes.4bii: Most answers to this part were not specific enough. The most common incorrect answer was ‘5 minutes’.
notes.4iii: This part was answered very well.
notes.4iv: Most candidates answered this part well and could draw the correct line on to the graph for a higher temperature. A few candidates drew the line above or below this.
notes.4c: Many candidiates were unable to decide whether ‘larger pieces of zinc’ would have a ‘higher’ or ‘lower’ surface area.
notes.4d: (i) Some answers for this showed that candidates understood ‘electrolysis’ and especially the electrolysis of ‘molten ionic compounds’. Some candidates dot the answers the wrong way round and others gave ‘chloride’ rather than ‘chlorine’.
notes.4dii: This was a very poorly answered question, with many candidates forgetting that graphite is used because it is ‘inert’.
notes.5: Candidates found some of the parts in this question the most challenging, particularly parts (b)(i), (ii) and especially (d) and (e)(i). Many candidates could not draw ‘a ring around the carboxylic acid functional group’ and so did not attempt it at all in part (a). Many also suggested that Na CO was sodium carbon oxide in part 2 3
notes.5c: Most candidates gave ‘water’ but did not give ‘sodium carbonate’ for a completely correct answer. The incorrect answer ‘sodium carbon oxide’ was common.
notes.5a: Many candidates struggled with this answer and could not identify the ‘carboxylic acid functional group’ and so did not attempt to answer the question at all. Some candidates thought that it also had a ‘carbon-carbon double bond’ in its structure.
notes.5b: (i) Candidates misunderstood the term ‘unsaturated’ and so not many correct answers were seen here. A few candidates described ‘unsaturated’ in terms of solutes and solutions which was not appropriate in this question.
notes.5bii: Generally chemical tests were not well recalled. Few candidates knew that ‘bromine water’ was the correct reagent and that it went ‘colourless’. Some thought that it became ‘orange’.
notes.5d: Many candidates struggled to use the words in the correct context. Many thought that ‘ethene joined with a monomer’ instead of it being the monomer and few used ‘polymerisation’ in the correct context.
notes.5e: (i) This was a very challenging question for most candidates. Many candidates did not read the question correctly and talked about chromatography instead of obtaining ‘a solution of this mixture of pigments from balsam flowers’. Some candidates incorrectly suggested ‘distillation’.
notes.5eii: Candidates were able to read the chromatogram successfully in this question. Some thought one pigment was present instead of two.
notes.6: Candidates did well on this question, particularly on parts (a), (b)(ii) and (e)(i). They did well on questions where they were using information from the table. Candidates were often unable to recall properties of transition metal compounds in part (c) and the chemical test in part (e)(ii). Most candidates knew some information about alloys for the longer part (f).
notes.6a: This question was answered very well. If it is stated as ‘very good’ in the table, it is best to use these words in the answer and not just ‘good’.
notes.6b: (i) Lots of candidates talked about ‘it’ or ‘they’ and did not name ‘aluminium’ or ‘steel’ which led to confused responses.
notes.6bii: This part was very well answered. Most candidates could interpret the information in the table and gave correct answers.
notes.6c: Candidates did not recall the properties of transition metals and many talked about density and conductivity of the compounds instead of comparing the colours of them.
notes.6d: Most could get ‘silver’ and ‘lithium’ as the ‘least’ and ‘most’ reactive respectively but got ‘aluminium’ and ‘magnesium’ confused.
notes.6e: (i) This was probably the best answered question on the paper. Most candidates gave ‘reversible’ as the correct answer here.
notes.6eii: The chemical tests were poorly recalled and the ‘test for hydrogen’ was no exception. Some candidates thought that a ‘glowing splint’ went ‘pop’ and many did not know or attempt the question.
notes.6f: Many candidates knew what an alloy was. Some incorrectly said that ‘metals bonded’ or ‘joined’ together. ‘Why alloys are used instead of pure iron’ was answered very well and many candidates were able to state one ‘use of an alloy of iron’.
notes.7: In part (b)(i) candidates were often unable to give the correct state. Parts (b)(ii) and (iv) were not well answered. There were many good answers for part (a) and most were able to quote ‘the density of bromine’ successfully in part (b)(iii)..
notes.7a: This question was successfully attempted. Some candidates did not mention ‘particles’.
notes.7b: (i) Many candidates could not deduce that the state would be a ‘liquid’.
notes.7bii: Quite a few candidates correctly stated ‘increases down the group’ here. There were some answers that described density and numbers of electrons so did not answer this specific question.
notes.7iii: This question was well answered and most candidates wrote down a correct figure for the density of bromine that was inside the range needed.
notes.7iv: Most candidates wrote down the electronic configuration of chlorine which does not answer the question.
notes.7c: (i) Most candidates remembered that iodine is diatomic. ‘2I’ was still seen as a common error.
notes.7cii: Many candidates incorrectly talked about the reactivity of potassium instead of bromine.
notes.7d: There were quite a few candidates that did not attempt this part and some candidates used atomic numbers instead of mass numbers.
notes.key_messages:
• Questions requiring simple answers to structure and bonding were usually answered well, as were
questions involving balancing equations and reaction rates.
• Questions on more detailed aspects of practical procedures (e.g. crystallisation) need to contain a
more focused explanation and attention to detail.
• Some candidates need more practice on answering questions requiring extended answers e.g.
notes.general_comments:
Many candidates showed a very good knowledge of Core Chemistry. Good responses were shown
throughout the paper. Nearly all candidates were entered at the appropriate level. The general standard of
answering was comparable with previous years.
